entities.name: Lucius Valerius Catullus Messalinus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Valerius Catullus Messalinus, a prominent Roman senator during the Flavian dynasty, achieved notoriety as the most feared and ruthless *delator*, or informer, of his age, symbolizing the oppressive climate of Emperor Domitian's later reign. His career, spanning the late 1st century CE, saw him rise to consul *suffectus* twice, in 73 CE and again in 85 CE, yet it was his relentless pursuit of alleged enemies of the state, often on charges of *maiestas* (treason), that etched his name into the annals of Roman infamy. Contemporaries like Tacitus and Juvenal vividly portrayed his terrifying persona, exacerbated by his blindness, which paradoxically seemed to sharpen his malevolent focus and immunity to visual distractions or pleas.

Messalinus leveraged the system of *delatio* to devastating effect, accumulating vast wealth through the confiscation of property from those he successfully prosecuted. He played a central role in the purges that targeted intellectuals and senators perceived as threats to Domitian's increasingly autocratic rule. Notable victims of this period, often linked to Messalinus's machinations, included figures like Helvidius Priscus, whose steadfast republicanism was deemed seditious, and the Stoic opposition figures Arulenus Rusticus and Herennius Senecio. His participation in the infamous 'council of the turbot' recounted in Juvenal's 'Satire IV' further cemented his image as a fawning yet dangerous courtier, whose opinions carried deadly weight.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Lucius Valerius Catullus Messalinus was a central figure in the oppressive political climate of Domitian's reign, orchestrating the downfall of numerous prominent Romans and contributing to the widespread fear among the elite. His actions profoundly shaped the experience of Roman governance in the late 1st century CE and served as a stark example of imperial terror.
